issues.description: The main text states the track is '1-meter long' and speed is 'calculated as 1m/descent time,' but the Methods section specifies that the two push-button switches (start/end) are 'located 92 cm apart.' If the timed distance is 92 cm but speed is calculated using 1 m, all reported speeds are systematically overestimated by approximately 8.7%. This affects absolute speed values, the reported optimization percentage, and the relationship to the stated maximum possible speed.
issues.quote: a wheel that traveled down a 1-meter long inclined track... The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time)

issues.description: The results section states 'the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h,' but the payoff formula in the Methods uses MaxSpeed = 160. This creates an inconsistency: either participants could never achieve the theoretical payoff maximum (since the actual max is ~154), or the reported maximum speed of 154 is incorrect. This also affects the interpretation of the 71% optimization claim and the incentive structure for participants.
issues.quote: the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h... with MaxSpeed = 160, MinSpeed = 96

issues.description: The paper inconsistently uses '95% Confidence Intervals' and '95% Highest Posterior Density Intervals' when reporting results from Bayesian models. For Bayesian analyses, the appropriate term is credible interval (or HPDI), not confidence interval—these have fundamentally different interpretations. The switching between terms within the same paragraph is confusing and suggests possible confusion about the inferential framework.
issues.quote: Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02)... average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h (95% Highest Posterior Density Interval: (117.3, 130.6))

issues.description: The Generation × Treatment interaction for understanding has a 95% CI of (0.03, 0.81), which excludes zero, indicating a credible positive interaction effect. Yet the authors conclude 'these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects... individual understanding.' By the authors' own inferential criterion (95% credible intervals), this interaction is credible. The authors acknowledge 'participants in the very last generation had a slightly better understanding when they had inherited a theory' but then dismiss this finding, which is internally inconsistent.
issues.quote: Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (0.03, 0.81), mean = 0.44... Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.description: The study equates 'causal understanding' with the ability to make correct explicit predictions on a 10-item forced-choice test covering only two dimensions. However, causal understanding is a richer construct that includes implicit/intuitive knowledge, understanding of interactions between variables, and procedural know-how. The authors themselves note that participants 'did not randomly explore the parameter space' and had 'appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration,' which suggests implicit causal knowledge that their measure fails to capture. The cognitive niche hypothesis primarily concerns reasoning abilities broadly, not just explicit verbal/propositional knowledge.
issues.quote: participants did not randomly explore the parameter space... This indicates that participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration

issues.subcategory: understanding test limited to single-dimension pairs
issues.description: The understanding test only presents pairs of wheels varying along a single dimension (either inertia or centre of mass), never both simultaneously. This fails to assess understanding of the tradeoff between the two dimensions, which is arguably the most important aspect of causal understanding for this task. A participant could score perfectly yet have no understanding of how the two dimensions interact, which is the core optimization challenge.
issues.quote: The test comprised 10 pairs of wheels: 5 in which wheels varied in their moment of inertia, 5 in which wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass.

issues.description: The experimenter manually positioned weights on the physical wheel and was not blind to experimental condition. Since the experimenter could see which treatment a participant was in and could see their configuration choices, there is potential for subtle experimenter demand effects (e.g., speed of setup, nonverbal cues, precision of weight placement). This is especially concerning because 'Data collection was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.'
issues.quote: the experimenter positioned the weights on the physical wheel accordingly... Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.description: No formal power analysis was conducted. The justification is that sample sizes are 'larger than those reported in previous publications,' but this does not ensure adequate statistical power to detect meaningful effects, particularly for the treatment comparison (hypothesis 2), where the key question is whether theory transmission affects performance and understanding. With only 14 chains per treatment, the study may be underpowered to detect moderate effects of theory transmission, and the null result could reflect insufficient power rather than a true null.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications

issues.description: The preregistered model for Analysis 4 (comparing understanding across treatments) did not converge, so the authors modified the analysis by aggregating scores and removing terms associated with 'Physical Principle.' While the deviation is disclosed, the model non-convergence may itself be informative (e.g., indicating model misspecification or complex data structure). The alternative model changes the research question from examining dimension-specific understanding to examining aggregate understanding, which loses important information given the central finding that understanding is dimension-specific.
issues.quote: the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable 'Physical Principle' in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc exploratory analyses with small subgroups
issues.description: The analyses examining how inherited theory type affects exploration and understanding (Figure 3) are explicitly labeled as exploratory but involve very small subgroups: N=15 (inertia theory), N=17 (centre-of-mass theory), N=6 (full theory), and N=18 (irrelevant theory). With only 6 participants inheriting a full theory, conclusions about this group are highly uncertain. Additionally, the categorization of 'Configurations' treatment participants into those producing 'various,' 'balanced,' or 'unbalanced' wheels involves post-hoc grouping criteria that are not specified.
issues.quote: The few participants who inherited a full theory (N = 6) produced compact and asymmetrical wheels (D-H).

issues.description: Cohen's kappa is designed for assessing agreement between exactly two raters. The study used 5 raters to code theories, so Fleiss' kappa (or Light's kappa as averaged pairwise Cohen's kappa) would be appropriate. The text reports 'Cohen's kappa coefficients' without clarifying whether these are averages of pairwise comparisons or some other aggregation. Additionally, the method for resolving disagreements among the 5 raters is not described.
issues.quote: 5 individuals blind to the research question... Cohen's kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters (0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).

issues.description: The paper does not report prior distributions used in the Bayesian models, the number of MCMC chains, iterations, warmup periods, or convergence diagnostics (e.g., R-hat values, trace plots) in the main text. These are essential for evaluating the reliability of Bayesian analyses. The authors note that for Analysis 3, 'the chains were inefficient and the effective number of samples for one parameter was low,' which raises concerns about the reliability of the primary treatment comparison.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.subcategory: MCMC convergence problems acknowledged but not fully addressed
issues.description: Analysis 3, which is the central comparison between treatments, had inefficient MCMC chains and low effective sample sizes. While the authors mention running 'additional models' that 'confirmed the reported results,' the details of what was changed to improve convergence are not provided in the main text. Problems with MCMC convergence suggest potential model misspecification or data issues that should be more thoroughly addressed.
issues.quote: For this model, the chains were inefficient and the effective number of samples for one parameter was low (see Supplementary Table 3). The robustness of the model estimates was checked by running additional models.

issues.subcategory: assignment of zero speed to failed wheels
issues.description: Wheels that did not descend were assigned a speed of 0. This is an arbitrary choice that could introduce artifacts if failure rates differ systematically across generations or treatments. Failure likely has a different generative process than slow descent, and treating it as speed=0 conflates two distinct outcomes. An alternative approach (e.g., analyzing failure rates separately, using hurdle/zero-inflated models, or analyzing only successful wheels) might better capture the data-generating process. The restriction to 'last two trials' to reduce failures also discards potentially informative data.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0. Data were restricted to participants' last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.

issues.description: Chains contained exclusively male or exclusively female participants, but no analysis examines whether sex affected performance, understanding, theory generation, or exploration patterns. With 70 men and 70 women split into sex-segregated chains, sex is perfectly confounded with chain identity and could contribute to between-chain variance. At minimum, sex should be included as a covariate or its effects examined.
issues.quote: participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females)

issues.description: The sample consists entirely of French university students, a highly educated WEIRD population. The authors acknowledge this limitation regarding exploration biases but do not adequately discuss how education level, familiarity with experimental settings, or cultural background might affect the core findings about the relationship between causal understanding and cultural evolution. Furthermore, the generalization from a 2-dimensional optimization problem to 'complex technologies' like bows, houses, and kayaks involves an enormous leap in complexity that is insufficiently justified.
issues.quote: Future cross-cultural work involving non WEIRD participants should tell us whether this selective exploration is culturally constructed or shared across populations

issues.description: With only 5 generations per chain, the study captures a very limited amount of cultural evolution. Real cumulative cultural evolution occurs over hundreds or thousands of generations. The study demonstrates initial optimization but cannot speak to whether causal understanding becomes important at later stages, whether optimization plateaus without understanding, or whether understanding eventually emerges given enough generations. The strong conclusion that 'complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning' extends well beyond what 5 generations can demonstrate.
issues.quote: Participants were organized into chains of 5 individuals... These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

issues.subcategory: false dichotomy between cognitive and cultural niche hypotheses
issues.description: The paper frames the cognitive niche hypothesis and cultural niche hypothesis as competing alternatives, but they are not mutually exclusive. The cognitive niche hypothesis does not claim that causal understanding is necessary for ALL technological improvement—only that enhanced cognition contributed significantly to human technological success. Showing that some optimization occurs without explicit understanding does not refute the cognitive niche hypothesis, as cognitive abilities (including implicit reasoning evident in participants' non-random exploration) may still be essential contributors. The authors' own finding that participants showed 'appropriate intuitions' actually supports a role for cognition.
issues.quote: According to the cognitive niche hypothesis, natural selection enhanced our ancestors' ability to think creatively, plan and engage in causal reasoning... The cultural niche hypothesis suggests that complex technologies like bows result from the accumulation of many, mostly small, often poorly understood improvements

issues.subcategory: confound between theory content and exploration constraint
issues.description: The finding that inherited theories constrain exploration is presented as evidence that theories are detrimental. However, the causal direction is ambiguous: theories that direct attention to one dimension could be beneficial if that dimension is more important, and the 'constraint' could be efficient specialization rather than a limitation. Additionally, the comparison between theory-inheriting and non-theory-inheriting participants is confounded by treatment assignment (between-subjects), so other treatment differences could contribute.
issues.quote: inheriting a theory mostly constrained participants' exploration, and prevented them from noticing the effects of relevant variables outside of the theory they received

issues.description: All 10 pairs of wheels in the understanding test were presented in the same fixed order to all participants. This introduces potential order effects, learning effects within the test, or fatigue effects that could systematically bias scores. Counterbalancing or randomizing the order across participants would have controlled for these confounds.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.description: The paper mentions that some wheels failed to descend and shows failure bars in Figure 2, but does not report the exact number or proportion of failures by generation, treatment, or trial in the text. Failure rates could systematically differ between conditions and generations, and this information is needed to evaluate the robustness of the speed results (especially since failed wheels were coded as speed = 0).
issues.quote: Vertical bars show the number of wheels that did not descend (i.e. failures) at each trial in each treatment.

issues.description: With 5 raters coding theories, disagreements are inevitable even with high kappa values. The paper does not describe how disagreements were resolved (e.g., majority vote, discussion to consensus, adjudication by a sixth rater). The final categorization of theories directly affects the exploratory analyses in Figure 3.
issues.quote: 5 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel... and were asked to code participants' theories

issues.description: In the Configurations + Theory treatment, participants wrote their theory after completing the understanding test. The test itself could have influenced theory content by priming participants to think about specific dimensions (inertia or centre of mass). Since the test systematically presents both dimensions, it could have shaped the theories transmitted to subsequent generations, creating an artificial boost in theory quality relative to what participants would have spontaneously generated.
issues.quote: Participants were asked to write their theory after the test phase was completed.

issues.subcategory: understanding score chance level not specified
issues.description: The understanding test allows three responses per pair (Wheel 1, Wheel 2, No difference). The expected chance-level score depends on which responses are correct and whether 'No difference' is ever correct. With 3 response options and 10 questions, random guessing gives an expected score of 3.33 (if exactly one option is always correct). This baseline is shown as a horizontal line in figures but is never explicitly stated or justified in the text.
issues.quote: Horizontal line shows expected score for random guessers.

issues.subcategory: cannot distinguish cumulative improvement from individual learning within 5 trials
issues.description: Each participant had 5 trials, and the transmitted information came from the previous participant's last 2 trials (presumably their best configurations). Performance increases across generations could partly reflect a ratchet effect from always transmitting late-trial (better) configurations, rather than genuine cumulative cultural improvement requiring inter-generational transmission. The design does not include a control condition without cultural transmission (e.g., isolated individuals with 25 trials) to distinguish individual learning from cultural accumulation.
issues.quote: Each participant had 5 trials to minimize the time it took for the wheel to reach the end of the track. All participants (except those in the first generation) were provided with the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in their chain

issues.description: Only the last two configurations and scores are transmitted between generations. This minimal transmission protocol may understate the potential benefits of causal understanding—in real cultural evolution, much richer information (demonstrations, explanations, apprenticeships) is transmitted. By restricting theory transmission to ≤340 characters, the study may create conditions that artificially favor non-understanding-based optimization by preventing detailed causal knowledge from being effectively communicated.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with 'The wheel covers the distance faster when...'

issues.description: The claim of '71% optimization after only four cultural generations' is not accompanied by an explicit formula. If calculated as (Gen5 - Gen1)/(Max - Gen1) = (145.7 - 123.6)/(154 - 123.6) = 72.7%, the reported 71% is approximate but not exact. Additionally, using a minimum speed baseline (e.g., MinSpeed = 96 from the payoff formula) would give a very different optimization percentage. The ambiguity in calculation method prevents readers from verifying this key claim.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.
